title: Interactive Demo for Account Executives Playbook
summary: A stage-by-stage guide to the interactive demo for account executives, from first call to renewal, plus a selector to match demo format to deal stage.
body_markdown:
The strategic case for account executives owning their demos is settled: reps who carry a reusable, personalizable interactive demo out-sell reps who wait on a scarce sales engineer. This piece assumes you already buy that argument. What it gives you instead is the tactical layer: the exact scripts, templates, checklists, and objection plays you can copy into your next call, plus a repeatable way to build and maintain the demo library that powers all of them.


Think of this as the field kit that sits underneath the workflow. If you want the stage-by-stage strategy of where each demo fits across a deal, start with our[interactive demo for account executives workflow guide](https://www.storylane.io/blog/interactive-demo-account-executives) . Come back here when you need the words to say and the assets to build.


> **What you will walk away with:** a six-item library-build checklist, a live-personalization script you can run verbatim, an objection-to-navigation map, three follow-up templates, and a weekly maintenance routine that keeps the whole kit from going stale.


## Build Your AE Demo Library First: A 6-Item Checklist


Every play below draws on one thing: a small, reusable library you assemble once and pull from forever. The best AEs I know do not build a demo per deal. They build a home base, then re-cut from it in minutes. That is the difference between an hour of prep and five.


- "I want every AE to have a curated 'home base' of interactive walkthroughs so they don't have to start from scratch every time they get a new lead." (Director of Sales Enablement, logistics)


Use this checklist to stand up your home base before your next call:


- **Capture your three highest-win flows.** Record the product paths that close deals most often, not every feature. Three tight flows beat thirty stale ones.
- **Build one "core value" demo per persona.** A champion, an economic buyer, and a technical evaluator each need a different opening, so cut three versions from the same recording.
- **Templatize the personalizable fields.** Mark logo, company name, sample data, and industry so you can swap them in seconds later.
- **Write a one-line "why this matters" per step.** Your hotspot copy should sell the outcome, not narrate the click.
- **Keep every flow under 12 steps.** Long walkthroughs lose people. If a flow runs past 12 steps, split it into two demos.
- **Version and date each demo.** Retire anything showing a feature you no longer support, so you never present a stale screen.


If you are building your first library from zero, our guide on[how to create an interactive product demo](https://www.storylane.io/blog/how-to-create-an-interactive-product-demo) walks through capture and hotspot writing in detail. The point of the library is repeatability: you invest once, then every new lead starts you at step five instead of step one.


## The Live Personalization Script (Copy This Into Your Next Call)


Personalization is what separates a demo from a screen-share, and the AEs who win do it live, on the call, without pinging anyone.


- "Being able to swap out the prospect's logo or key data points on the fly while we are on the Zoom call makes the experience feel much more tailored without needing an engineer to build a custom environment." (Account Executive, advertising tech)


Here is the exact sequence I coach reps to run, with the words to say at each beat:


1. **Confirm context in the first two minutes.** Say: "Before I show anything, what team do you run and what's the one metric you're measured on this quarter?" Map their answer to the flow you will open.
2. **Load the persona-matched demo from your library.** Do not open the product cold. Open the version you already cut for their role.
3. **Swap the visible identity live.** As you talk, change the logo and company name to theirs: "Let me put your name on this so it reads like your account, not a generic sandbox."
4. **Replace sample data with numbers they recognize.** Use their team size, their region, or a figure they gave you in discovery.
5. **Drive to the one outcome they came for.** Every click should push toward the result they named, not a feature tour.
6. **Pause on the "aha" screen.** Stop talking, let them react, and note which screen earned the reaction.


The technique matters more than the tool, but the tool has to allow live edits without a rebuild. If you are still comparing options, our roundup of the[best product tour software](https://www.storylane.io/blog/product-tour-software) covers which platforms support in-call editing. Personalization done live also signals competence: it tells the buyer you understand their world well enough to show it back to them.


## The Objection-to-Navigation Map: Answer Doubts Inside the Product


Objections during a demo are not interruptions. They are buying signals, and the AE who answers them by navigating to proof wins trust a slide can never earn. The play is preparation, not improvisation: before the call, list the five objections you hear most and pre-load a screen or side flow that answers each one.


Below is the objection map I hand to new reps. Print it, keep it beside your notes, and rehearse the navigations until they are muscle memory.


Objection heard on the call AE response, inside the demo


"Does it integrate with our stack?" Jump to the integrations screen and filter to their exact tool by name.


"This looks complex for my team." Open the simplest end-user view and complete one task in under three clicks.


"Can it handle our data volume?" Load a data-heavy view and let them scroll it live rather than describing it.


"How is this different from what we use now?" Navigate to the one screen your incumbent cannot produce and stop there.


"I need to see reporting." Open the dashboard, swap in a metric they named, and let them read it.


Notice that every response is a navigation, not a sentence. When a buyer sees you move to the exact screen that answers their doubt, the objection converts into a proof point in real time. That is only possible when the AE, not a distant SE, controls the environment.


Two coaching notes make the map sharper. First, name the objection out loud before answering it: "You want to know this won't blow up your admin's week, let me show you." That earns credit for listening, then the screen does the convincing. Second, read the pattern. A buyer who asks about integrations once usually wants reassurance, and a quick filtered view settles it. A buyer who keeps returning to the same doubt is telling you where the deal actually lives, so slow down there.


## Three Follow-Up Templates That Turn a Demo Into a Leave-Behind


The call ends, and most reps send a recap email no one reopens. The interactive demo you just ran should leave the call with the buyer as a living asset, not a PDF. Here are three copy-ready templates for the moments that matter most.


**Template 1: the same-day leave-behind.** Lead with the demo link, not the attachment. "Thanks for the time today. Here's the exact walkthrough we looked at, with your data still in it, so you can revisit the \[outcome\] screen whenever you like: \[link\]. Docs are below if you want them." Trim the shared flow to the three screens that earned reactions.


**Template 2: the multi-thread forward.** When your champion has to sell internally, hand them a proxy. "You mentioned you'll need to bring \[VP\] along. I've built a short version that opens straight on \[the outcome they care about\], secure link here: \[link\]. Forward it as is, it's branded to your team." Build a stakeholder-specific version: the economic buyer's flow opens on ROI, the technical evaluator's opens on security and integrations.


**Template 3: the re-engagement nudge.** When engagement data shows a stakeholder reopened the demo, time your outreach to it: "Saw the \[reporting\] view got a second look on your side, happy to walk whoever's asking through it live for fifteen minutes." Let the click, not a guess, trigger the send.


For inspiration on what a polished leave-behind looks like before you build yours,[see real interactive demo examples](https://www.storylane.io/blog/awesome-interactive-demo-examples) . The leave-behind is where an AE's leverage compounds: the same asset that ran the live call now works the buyer's internal hallways while the rep sleeps. Track who opens and what they click, and you also get a map of the buying committee, telling you whose objection to solve next.


## The Expansion Play: One Demo, Re-Cut for Renewal


The demo does not retire at closed-won. The most under-used expansion play I know is showing an existing customer the product they already pay for but do not use.


- "We struggle with upsell because our existing customers still think we only do what they bought two years ago; using interactive demos to show them the new features they aren't using yet is essential for our expansion strategy." (Customer Success Manager, enterprise software)


The play, step by step: pull the relevant flows from your library, re-cut a single demo of the two or three premium or newly shipped features the account has never seen, and send it two to three weeks before the renewal conversation, not during it. That reframes the call from a defensive price negotiation into a discussion about what more they could be getting.


Here is why it pays, with assumptions stated. Say a customer sits on a base plan worth 20,000 dollars a year, and a premium tier adds 8,000 dollars a year. Run this play across 25 comparable accounts and land just 4 of them, and that is 32,000 dollars of net-new recurring revenue from a demo you already had the pieces to build. No SE hours, no new content budget, one afternoon of assembly, because the flows already exist in your library. You are re-cutting, not rebuilding.


The same motion works for quarterly business reviews. Instead of a slide summarizing usage, drop in a short interactive walkthrough of one feature the account has ignored and let the champion click through it live. Expansion stops feeling like a pitch and starts feeling like the customer discovering value they already paid to unlock.


## Keep the Kit Sharp: A Weekly Maintenance Routine


A demo library is only an asset if it stays current. Scripts drift, features ship, and a stale screen in front of a prospect undoes the trust the rest of the demo built. Treat maintenance as a standing habit, not a cleanup you do when something breaks.


- **Version and date every flow.** Retire anything showing a feature you no longer support the day it changes.
- **Prune to your highest-completion flows each quarter.** If you track one metric, track completion rate by flow. It tells you which walkthroughs earn attention and which lose it, and it points directly at the screens to cut.
- **Hold demos to roughly 10 to 12 steps.** Past that, completion falls off a cliff. Write hotspots in 15 to 18 words, long enough to sell the outcome, short enough to read at a glance.
- **Treat 80% completion as your floor for a leave-behind.** If a flow underperforms that, it is too long or the first screen is not earning the second click.
- **Refresh objection navigations when the product moves.** If the integrations screen or dashboard changes, re-walk your objection map so every navigation still lands.


These are guardrails I offer as opinion, drawn from watching thousands of demos perform, not borrowed statistics. The discipline they enforce is the real benchmark: short, outcome-led, and finishable beats comprehensive every time. A rep who prunes to their strongest flows every quarter compounds a real advantage over one who never looks at the data.


## When to Hand the Play to a Sales Engineer


None of this makes the SE obsolete, and the tactical kit has a clear boundary. If the buyer's next question is "does it fit my workflow," the AE owns the demo. If it becomes "prove it works against our production data and our custom stack," bring the SE into the room. Deep, custom-integration proofs with a technical audience genuinely benefit from an expert live. A first discovery call with a champion does not, and forcing an SE into it just recreates the bottleneck.


Owning the routine 80% with the scripts and templates above is exactly what frees your SEs for the technical 20% where they change outcomes. That is the honest line between the two roles.


## FAQ


**What scripts should an AE prepare before a live demo?**


Three: a two-minute context-confirmation opener that surfaces the buyer's team and key metric, a live-personalization narration for swapping logo and data on the call, and an objection-to-navigation map that turns the five doubts you hear most into on-screen proof. Rehearse the navigations until they are muscle memory so you move to the right screen without hunting.


**How do I build an AE demo library from scratch?**


Record your three highest-win product paths, cut one core-value version per persona from those recordings, templatize the personalizable fields (logo, company name, sample data, industry), keep every flow under 12 steps, and version and date each one. Assemble once, then re-cut per deal in minutes instead of building fresh every time.


**How should an AE handle objections during a demo?**


Answer inside the product, not with a promise. Pre-load a screen or side flow for each common objection, name the objection out loud before responding, then navigate straight to the proof. A filtered integrations view settles an integration question, and the simplest end-user view answers a complexity worry in under three clicks.


**What should an AE send as a demo follow-up?**


Lead with the personalized demo link, not an attachment. Send the exact flow you ran with their logo and data still in it, trimmed to the three screens that earned reactions, and put one clear next step inside the demo. For multi-threading, build a stakeholder-specific version per buying role and let your champion forward the secure link.


**How often should an AE update their demo library?**


Version and date flows continuously and retire stale screens the day a feature changes. Do a deeper pass each quarter: prune to your highest-completion flows, re-walk your objection navigations against the current product, and cut anything running past 12 steps. Completion rate by flow is the metric that tells you what to keep.


## Key Takeaways


- Build the AE demo library first: three highest-win flows, one version per persona, templatized fields, everything under 12 steps and dated.
- Run the live-personalization script verbatim: confirm context, load the persona demo, swap identity and data live, drive to one outcome, pause on the aha.
- Answer objections by navigating to proof, using a pre-built objection-to-navigation map instead of promising a follow-up.
- Turn every call into a leave-behind with three follow-up templates: same-day, multi-thread forward, and re-engagement nudge.
- Re-cut library flows into a pre-renewal expansion demo to surface unused features at almost no extra cost.
- Maintain the kit weekly: version, prune to highest-completion flows, hold to 10 to 12 steps, refresh objection navigations when the product moves.
- Hand deeply technical, custom-integration proofs to a sales engineer; own the routine majority yourself.
